options: For each node, the list of nodes it connects to
A sorted list of all edges by weight
A table of every pair of nodes
The order a DFS visits the nodes
why: It is the usual way to write a graph in code: `{ A: ['B', 'C'], ... }`.

q: Why does graph code need a `seen` set?
options: To sort the nodes
A graph can have loops, and without it the search never stops
To make the search find the shortest path
Graphs cannot be stored without it
why: In my test, with no `seen` the queue held 105 entries after 40 steps and kept growing.

q: Which search finds the fewest edges between two nodes when every edge counts as 1?
options: DFS
Either one, the same way
BFS
Neither, you need sorting
why: BFS visits the closest nodes first, so the first time it reaches a node it used the fewest edges.

q: In BFS, when should you mark a node as seen?
options: When you take it out of the queue
After the whole search is finished
Never, the queue is enough
When you add it to the queue
why: If you wait until you take it out, the same node can be added twice (7 pushes instead of 6 in my test).

q: How do you count the islands in a grid?
options: Scan the cells. At each new land cell count 1, then spread over the joined land and mark it
Count all the land cells
Sort the rows and count the groups
Count the water cells next to land
why: The grid is a graph. Each new unseen land cell starts one island, and the search marks the rest of it.

q: Course schedule with a counter of waiting tasks: how do you know there is a cycle?
options: The queue is full at the start
The order ends up with fewer nodes than the graph
A node has indegree 0
The graph has more edges than nodes
why: Nodes in a cycle wait for each other, so they never reach 0 and never join the order.
